'''Leonard Moos Rieser''' (May 18, 1922 – December 15, 1998) was an American physicist who worked on the [[Manhattan Project]] and later for [[nuclear disarmament]]. Rieser was a professor of physics and provost at [[Dartmouth College]].

== Biography ==
Rieser was born May 18, 1922, in [[Chicago]].<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Leonard M. Rieser |url=https://history.aip.org/phn/11608031.html |access-date=2023-08-12 |website=[[American Institute of Physics]] |archive-date=November 7, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221107140536/https://history.aip.org/phn/11608031.html |url-status=live }}</ref> He studied at Dartmouth College from 1940 to 1942 before transferring to the [[University of Chicago]] and graduating with a [[bachelor's degree]] in physics in 1943.<ref name=":0">{{Cite press release |date=1998-12-17 |title=Leonard M. Rieser 1922–1998 |url=http://www.dartmouth.edu/~news/releases/1998/dec98/rieser.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160310002123/http://www.dartmouth.edu/~news/releases/1998/dec98/rieser.html |access-date=2023-08-12 |website=Dartmouth News |publisher=[[Dartmouth College]] |archive-date=2016-03-10}}</ref> In 1942 he enlisted in the [[Army Signal Corps]] and after graduating from Chicago was assigned to work on the secret Manhattan Project, developing the [[Atomic Bomb|atomic bomb]].<ref name=":1">{{Cite journal |last=Holton |first=Gerald |author-link=Gerald Holton |date=1972-02-18 |title=Leonard M. Rieser, President-Elect, 1972 |journal=[[Science (journal)|Science]] |language=en |volume=175 |issue=4023 |pages=796–797 |doi=10.1126/science.175.4023.796 |pmid=4550686 |issn=0036-8075 |doi-access=free |bibcode=1972Sci...175..796H }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> Rieser first worked at the [[Metallurgical Laboratory]] in Chicago, then at [[Los Alamos Laboratory]] in [[New Mexico]] where he witnessed the [[Trinity (nuclear test)|first atomic explosion]].<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> In 1944 he married Rosemary Littledale.<ref>{{Cite news |date=2012-12-11 |title=Rosemary Littledale Rieser |work=[[Valley News]] |url=https://www.vnews.com/Archives/2012/12/Rosemary-Rieser-obit-vn-121112 |issn=1072-6179 |access-date=August 12, 2023 |archive-date=August 12, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812210919/https://www.vnews.com/Archives/2012/12/Rosemary-Rieser-obit-vn-121112 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":1" />

Rieser left the army and Los Alamos in 1946 to begin postgraduate studies at [[Stanford University]], graduating with a PhD in 1952. That year he began teaching physics at Dartmouth College, where he worked until his retirement in 1992. He became an associate professor in 1957, and a professor in 1960.<ref name=":0" /> He held various administrative positions at the college, including provost and dean of the faculty.<ref name=":0" />

Rieser served as president of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] from 1972 to 1975.<ref name=":2">{{Cite news |last=McSherry Breslin |first=Meg |date=1998-12-19 |title=Leonard Rieser, Keeper of Doomsday Clock |work=[[Chicago Tribune]] |url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1998-12-19-9812190011-story.html |access-date=August 12, 2023 |archive-date=August 12, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812210914/https://www.chicagotribune.com/news/ct-xpm-1998-12-19-9812190011-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":0" /> He was chair of the board of the [[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]] from 1985 to 1998.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Saxon |first=Wolfgang |date=1998-12-19 |title=Leonard Rieser, 76, Opponent Of Arsenal He Helped Create |language=en |pages=C16 |work=[[New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1998/12/19/us/leonard-rieser-76-opponent-of-arsenal-he-helped-create.html |access-date=2023-08-12 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=August 12, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230812210912/https://www.nytimes.com/1998/12/19/us/leonard-rieser-76-opponent-of-arsenal-he-helped-create.html |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite journal |last=Moore |first=Mike |date=March 1999 |title=Leonard M Rieser, 1922–1998 |url=https://www.proquest.com/docview/197818892 |journal=[[Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists]] |volume=55 |issue=2 |pages=4–5 |doi=10.1080/00963402.1999.11460305 |bibcode=1999BuAtS..55b...4M |id={{ProQuest|197818892}} |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The Bulletin's Leonard M. Rieser Award for Young Authors bears his name.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://thebulletin.org/blog/whats-new-bulletin/yangyang-cheng-2017-leonard-m-rieser-award-winner|title=The 2017 Leonard M. Rieser Award Winner|date=December 19, 2017|work=Bulletin of the Atomic Scientists|access-date=June 19, 2018|language=en}}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref> Starting in 1985, he was the keeper of the Bulletin's symbolic [[Doomsday Clock]] and moved its minute hand to indicate how close or far away we were from the threat of [[nuclear annihilation]].<ref name=":2" />

Rieser died December 15, 1998, from [[pancreatic cancer]] at the [[Dartmouth–Hitchcock Medical Center|Dartmouth'''–'''Hitchcock Medical Center]] in [[Lebanon, New Hampshire]], at the age of 76.<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" />
